📜 The Syro-Egyptian Society of London

The volume shows John Lee, Esq., LL.D., F.R.S. repeatedly presiding in the chair, while other meetings were chaired by Isaac Cullimore and Samuel Sharpe. It is therefore a genuine learned-society research collection rather than a later miscellaneous anthology.

🔑 Polymath Continents and Civilizational Regions

I would place the geographical-polymath reach of this volume across three principal continents - Africa, Asia and Europe, with a very large number of subsidiary intellectual regions:
Africa - Egypt, the Nile Valley, Delta, Thebes, Memphis, Heliopolis, Sais, Naucratis, Abyssinia/Ethiopia.
Asia - Assyria, Babylonia, Mesopotamia, Nineveh, Kurdistan, Armenia, Hadhramaut, Yemen, Oman, Arabia, Syria, the Holy Land, Persia, India, Ceylon, Central Asian routes and China.
Europe - London, Rome, Paris, Hanover and the European learned societies through which Egyptian, Assyrian, geographical and linguistic evidence was exchanged.

The intellectual continent is even larger: Egyptology, Assyriology before full professionalization, biblical archaeology, sacred geography, classical history, epigraphy, philology, astronomy, hydrology, ancient engineering, geology, ethnography, numismatics, ecclesiastical history and comparative chronology.

⚠️ Powerful Specialist Abstract on: " Original Papers Read Before the Syro-Egyptian Society of London - Volume I, Parts I-II " 

The publication is unusually important because its pictures are arguments.

The full Horapollo plate does not function as decoration. It gathers dozens of actual graphic signs - birds, serpents, celestial forms, human figures, boats, quadrupeds, vessels, plants, abstract marks, cartouche-like enclosures and numerical arrangements - numbered for comparison with Sharpe's running commentary.

Likewise, the enormous two-sheet cuneiform apparatus reproduces a long rock inscription line by line and sets comparative passages beside it. The arrangement permits the eye to detect recurrent sequences, altered wedges, missing contacts, parallels between Mühlbach's and Schütz's copies, and differences in ductus that prose alone could never convey. The continuation sheet carries the same comparison through the remaining lines.
And the Hadhramaut map is another kind of document. It spatializes valleys, coast, settlements, routes and regional relationships that Plate subsequently uses to discuss ancient trade, Arabia, Egypt, India and the movement of Christianity eastward. Those materials deserve to sit at the center of the analysis.

Short Technical Construct

This book is best approached through six evidential instruments, each operating differently:
Stone preserves labor, titulary, damage, transport and religious succession. Sign preserves sound, concept, number, celestial reference and visual analogy. Wedge preserves scribal habit, linguistic differentiation, carving technique and inscriptional lineage. Landscape preserves vanished cities, trade corridors, imperial routes and ethnonyms.

Cycle preserves astronomical, hydrological and ritual time. 
Route preserves contact between civilizations that later historiography may falsely isolate.
The investigators repeatedly move from the smallest observable thing - one wedge, one hieroglyph, one damaged stone, one name, one river bend - toward much larger historical reconstructions.
That microscopic-to-macroscopic movement is where the volume becomes especially valuable.

Advanced Abstract / Analysis

The Original Papers Read Before the Syro-Egyptian Society of London preserve a remarkably experimental phase in Oriental antiquarian scholarship. Egyptian history, Assyrian archaeology, hieroglyphic interpretation, cuneiform decipherment, biblical geography, astronomy, hydrology, navigation, metallurgy, ancient engineering, numismatics, ecclesiastical history and ethnographic philology still occupy neighboring intellectual chambers. The volume's authors are therefore repeatedly able to notice evidence that would later be distributed among different professional specialties.

Its Egyptian studies are fundamentally material and graphic. Isaac Cullimore reads Manetho not simply as a chronology of kings but as evidence for changing territorial configurations - Pentarchy, Tetrarchy, Dyarchy, Monarchy and Dodekarchy - and explicitly intends his historical reconstruction to be clarified through a tabular arrangement of five Egyptian states and thirty dynasties synchronized with astronomical and Hebrew chronologies.

William Holt Yates moves from inscriptions into something approaching archaeological mechanics. At Aswan he records unfinished obelisks still lying in the quarries, gives their dimensions, compares the enormous masses at Baalbek, Luxor, Karnak and Rome, and asks the technological question that monument study inevitably raises: what tools, materials, transport systems and organizational knowledge permitted ancient builders to manipulate such masses?
This portion deserves much more attention than a conventional discussion of "obelisk symbolism." 

Yates is inadvertently opening several technical fields:
• experimental archaeology
• quarry archaeology
• ancient logistics
• lithotechnics
• fracture mechanics
• tool-mark analysis
• labor organization
• transportation engineering
• stone provenance
• monumental metrology
• archaeometallurgy

His observation of actual quarry scars is phenomenologically striking. He describes the ancient pick-mark as possessing an authenticity capable of bringing vanished labor almost sensorially into the present - one can nearly hear the ancient workmen. That passage is a genuine nineteenth-century precursor to what we might call archaeological presence studies.

Samuel Sharpe's Horapollo investigation is even more intellectually fertile than I allowed in the first treatment. Sharpe begins from the difficult status of Hieroglyphica: an alleged Egyptian explanatory tradition surviving in Greek, whose interpretations often appear figurative or linguistically confused. Rather than merely accepting or dismissing Horapollo, Sharpe compares each claim with signs identifiable on monuments.
That produces an early controlled comparison between inherited symbolic exegesis and deciphered graphic evidence.

The plate is indispensable. It contains fifty-eight numbered figures. Birds alternate with water-signs, boats, celestial forms, human figures, mammals, plants, utensils and geometric arrangements. 

These are therefore not illustrations appended after interpretation. They form a visual concordance. Sharpe repeatedly asks what relation exists among:
image - Egyptian word - Coptic survival - phonetic resemblance - astronomical object - mythic explanation - actual inscriptional usage.

For example, in his treatment of the year and month he connects the palm branch with the written expression for year, discusses the woman or cow in a boat associated with Isis and heliacal celestial phenomena, and examines the downward or upward horns of the moon as graphic information about lunar phases. Elsewhere he treats the hare in relation to opening or burrowing, the water-pot in titles associated with water, guardian figures, the numerical symbolism of sixteen in connection with desired Nile height, and the scribal assemblage of ink, sieve and reed.

That material opens far more than "Egyptian symbolism." It touches:
cognitive semiotics, embodied metaphor, rebus mechanics, iconophonetics, numerical symbolism, environmental semantics, graphic cognition, sacred scribal technology and the psychology of pictorial writing.

The cuneiform section is equally extraordinary.

The two large plates preserve a forty-line inscription and comparative passages. Grotefend cares about the shape of wedges, the angle at which strokes meet, their scale, spacing, recurrence, transformation, and whether strokes intersect at all.
He notices something exceptionally important: avoidance of intersecting wedges may arise partly from the material properties of the stone. Mühlbach observed unsound veins; intersecting strokes could encourage cracking. Grotefend therefore links orthography with the behavior of the carving medium.

That is already a primitive form of material palaeography.
The graphic system does not evolve solely in the abstract mind of scribes. Stone hardness, fissures, carving resistance, tool behavior and available writing surfaces exert pressure upon script morphology. That insight can now be carried considerably farther. The actual writing surfaces mentioned in the paper include rock, marble, brick, fragments, vessels and altar-like stones. 

Grotefend records different clay qualities, glazing, the location of inscriptions upon broad or narrow faces, wedge length, damaged signs and even an earthen vessel bearing sixty-three close rows of text.

Thus the paper contains the beginnings of an ecology of inscriptional media.

The Nineveh material also becomes richer when read beside the wedge paper. Ainsworth is confronting the archaeological problem that "Nineveh" may represent a metropolitan complex rather than one compact bounded settlement. He discusses Kouyunjik, Nimrud, Khorsabad, Athur, Baasheikha and Kalah Shergat and considers different chronological relationships among these sites.

That is an early problem in urban macro-archaeology.

The biblical layer is also much deeper than merely matching names. Ainsworth examines traditions about Asshur and Nimrod and brings Genesis into dialogue with local names, Arabic geographers, Xenophon, classical historical traditions, monumental inscriptions and Layard's discoveries. The paper notes that Arabic writers knew a ruined Athur connected with the Taurat and that early Assyrian monuments might lie beneath sites not yet fully explored.

The Trajan paper likewise demonstrates a highly developed geographical criticism. Ainsworth compares Dio Cassius, Strabo, Ptolemy, Pliny, Arabic and Kurdish place terminology and even the Targum of Onkelos on Genesis 8:4 in attempting to identify the Karduchian mountain zone. He then notices that the reported sequence of Trajan's march does not fit the actual relationship of Babylon, Ctesiphon, the Tigris and Euphrates, and uses geography to detect a historical narrative problem.

This is geographical falsification of textual narrative - using terrain to test whether a transmitted historical sequence is physically coherent.

Hadhramaut introduces yet another intellectual universe. Plate's map and essay connect Southern Arabia with incense and commerce, Egypt, India, the Queen of Sheba tradition, Red Sea navigation, Seleucia, Syriac Christianity and China. By his reading of the Xi'an monument, the Syriac lines contain clerical names and ecclesiastical offices, while the Chinese and Syriac dates can be reconciled by conversion from the Seleucid or "Greek" era.
Plate then makes an unusually advanced inference. 

If a priest could be sent from the ecclesiastical authority at Seleucia to investigate Christian communities in China, then communications must already have existed before his arrival; institutional knowledge of those communities had to travel westward before an emissary could be dispatched eastward.
That is almost network inference in the modern sense.

A surviving journey implies earlier communications that left no equally visible narrative record.
And Plate associates this ecclesiastical network with commerce. Hadhramaut becomes an intermediary between Egypt, Syria, Arabia, India and the further East.

This permits a major extension beyond Plate himself:
trade routes should be studied as carriers of manuscripts, liturgies, astronomical information, medicinal substances, scripts, cosmological stories, calendrical knowledge and theological vocabulary - not merely commodities.

Apparently people are also angry that I posted about Luma and played around with AI recently...

So again:

1) Luma was a nice little hobby thing on the side. Wicked is my main gig, obviously! Luma is a project I had in mind for almost a decade, built 2 prototypes of it already over the years (it's the project I showed to Oculus back in 2016 or so) and then did a gamejam where I finally solved the issues I got stuck on before.

It was the first game I was able to make with my 8 year old son. He and I played Minecraft together a lot and we talked about how one could make an even better game and that's how Luma jumped back into my mind.

And honestly, it was delightful to be able to make something with him. As a parent, it's amazing if you find something that you and your kid both get excited about. Him coming home from school with dozens of ideas and overflowing with creative energy was one of the best moments for me this year.

So, sue me if you get offended that I spent a bunch of time with my son being creative together. I posted about it online because it's just a genuinely good game already!

Here try it yourself: https://t.co/Xu3yzKOs8p
It's really good! 👍

2) I already made my stance on AI clear. No, we're not using any generative AI stuff on Wicked and people who now claim otherwise are just making shit up in a ridiculous fashion. AI at this stage isn't good enough to create assets or any such thing, not at the quality standards we require at Moon. Any good gamedev knows what AI can do and what it can't. And if they don't, they're not taking their jobs seriously.

But of course we're using AI to help with tooling, bugfixes and so on, like everyone else is. We'd be stupid not to. It's a genuinely useful tool.

3) A similar thing happened with https://t.co/JolbgwKsO7 - It's a database I built for myself and for our team to keep track of things early on. But then it became clear that most gamers would get a huge kick out of it, so I released it.

And since then, I got tons and tons and tons of messages from industry folks and players that they're using it every day now. We had like 300k visitors on the site now and people are daily driving it to help them find new games.

What is there to get outraged about? How about we let people have fun and celebrate if they have a good time?

The internet can be exhausting these days...

i genuinely did not expect a robot claw machine to make me think about ai differently but here we are.

been messing around with @axisrobotics for the past couple days. the pitch sounded off to me at first, control a virtual robot arm in your browser, no hardware, no download. 

felt like one of those crypto games where the “utility” is just an excuse to farm points. 

so i went in expecting nothing.

turns out every task you complete is a real recorded movement, timestamped, signed on chain, and actually used to train a robot to do that same thing in the real world. 

the reason it exists at all is kind of obvious once you sit with it. llms learned by reading the internet. 

robots don’t have an internet to learn from. nobody’s uploaded a million videos of “how to correctly grab a mug without dropping it” with the joint data attached. 

someone has to generate that from scratch, and apparently that someone can be me, on a laptop, at 1am.

what actually got me was the proof. 

their dataset didn’t just sit there, it pushed a real model from 83.9% to 88.8% success rate on an actual benchmark. 

that’s not marketing copy, that’s a published result. 

i’ve contributed real trajectories to that now and it’s a strange feeling knowing a robot somewhere might move a little better because of something i did on my laptop.

if you want to try it yourself, i’m using my link below, costs nothing but a few minutes and you get to see the whole thing live.

https://t.co/ZRkevwO0AW

This paper points out something that should have been obvious to all of us.

We’ve spent the last 2 years throwing massive diffusion models at offline RL actors just to handle multimodal data, and just pretending that a 50ms denoising loop per step is fine for robotics. 

The reality is it isn’t.

The argument of this paper is dead simple: the critic gets thrown away the second training ends. 

The actor is the only thing that actually has to run live on hardware. 

So why on earth are we stuffing all the compute into the actor?

People avoided deep critics before because offline value networks love to diverge into oblivion, but they managed to stabilize a deep residual critic using n-step targets and categorical cross-entropy. 

That lets the critic do the heavy lifting during training, so runtime is left to a tiny deterministic policy that runs in a single forward pass. 

It matches diffusion performance on OGBench while running 4x faster, no distillation hacks needed.

And i feel its genuinely a great work and definitely worth a read.

Read the full paper here: https://t.co/i0FVJuJUR2
